newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: APARTHEID POLICE MINISTER SAYS WILLING TO TESTIFY.
newsitem.headline: APARTHEID POLICE MINISTER SAYS WILLING TO TESTIFY.

text.p: An apartheid-era police minister said on Friday he would cooperate with South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission on human rights crimes, despite their threat to subpoena him to give evidence.

Adriaan Vlok, who was in charge of the police at the height of emergency rule in the mid-1980s, told national radio he had not been informed by the truth body of the pending summons and had learned of it through the media.

"I find it strange for a reconciliation committee to go about it this way getting people before them. It could have been done very easily, just by way of a telephone call or a letter calling upon me to assist them in certain matters," he said.
Nevertheless, Vlok said, he was still prepared to assist the commission.
"I have never refused to appear before them...I have declared myself prepared to go there voluntarily."

The truth commission's deputy chairman, Alex Boraine, told a news conference on Thursday that it would subpoena Vlok as well as eight former police generals on Friday to appear at closed hearings to tell all they know about abuses under apartheid.
He said Vlok's name was included because he had been named at a number of the commission's public hearings for victims of human rights violations.
"We will be asking him a number of questions about the allegations that have been made," Boraine said.
Vlok was police minister when hundreds of black activists were killed by police and up to 30,000 people were detained without charge amid countless allegations of torture in prisons.
It was unclear whether the summons had been issued against him by late Friday. Boraine declined on Friday to comment on Vlok's case, instead issuing a statement saying:
"The running of the subpoena process is now in the hands of the commission's investigative unit. We are not prepared to enter into speculation about the order and timing of the service of subpoenae."
The truth commission set up by President Nelson Mandela has the power to compensate victims of the war over apartheid and to grant amnesty to politically motivated perpetrators who confess.
